builds.title: The living shed roof: could a garden shed carry a meadow?
builds.dek: A garden shed topped with a deep, flowering meadow is a feed favorite; as filmed the roof carries about three times what it was framed for, but a shallow sedum roof on beefed-up rafters works.
builds.line: As filmed the soil weighs three times what the rafters can carry; a shallow, light sedum roof on stronger framing is a fine project.

builds.title: The backyard lazy river: can a pool pump make a current?
builds.dek: Reels show a trench dug around a yard, a liner laid in and a pool pump sending tubes drifting on a current; a pool pump barely stirs that much water, and the real thing needs a pump forty times bigger and drains that cannot trap a child.
builds.line: As filmed the water would barely move and the suction could trap a swimmer; built with block walls, a big low-head pump and a gravity collector tank, it is a real but costly project.

builds.title: The secret room under the floor: can you dig one through a trapdoor?
builds.dek: A living-room floor lifts away to reveal a hidden room dug out underneath, but the dig is about 100 tons of soil under your own foundation, so the version that works borrows space from a basement you already have.
builds.line: Digging a room under a lived-in house by hand is a cave-in waiting to happen; a hidden hatch into a room partitioned from an existing basement is a fun, legal build.

builds.title: The sunken fire pit with a moat: a backyard dream or a drowning hazard?
builds.dek: A circular conversation pit dug into the lawn, a fire in the middle and a ring of water around it is a reel favorite; as filmed it floods, and the moat is a hazard to children, but a drained pit with a pondless water ring works.
builds.line: The pit is buildable; the open moat and the missing drain are the problems, and both have fixes.

builds.title: The floating cabin on barrels sits lower than the reel lets on
builds.dek: A little cabin on a raft of blue drums drifting on a pond is a feed favorite, but a dozen barrels barely carry the cabin itself, and the real danger is a tip or a fall at night.
builds.line: On a dozen reused drums the cabin rides nearly awash and tips when friends step to the rail; on more than twice the flotation, wide and anchored, it is a sound pond cabin.

builds.title: The PVC hydroponic wall: lettuce, yes; strawberries, not like that
builds.dek: A garage wall of white pipes overflowing with lettuce and berries is a feed staple; the plumbing is real, but the tiny bucket, the berries in the pipes and the cord in the water need changing.
builds.line: As filmed the bucket runs dry in a day and the berries suffer; with a big tank, sloped channels for greens and a GFCI, it is a productive wall.

builds.title: The shipping container pool: is a steel box really a pool waiting to happen?
builds.dek: Reels show a used container with its roof sliced off, dropped in a hole and filled; the box was never built to hold water against its walls, but set above ground on an engineered frame it can make a sound lap pool.
builds.line: Buried and roofless as filmed, the box bows, rusts and can float out of the ground; set above ground on an engineered frame and lined, it is a real but pricey lap pool.

builds.title: The indoor waterfall wall: a calm feature or a humidifier you can't turn off?
builds.dek: A stone wall pouring a curtain of water into the living room looks serene, but at that flow it puts gallons of water into the air every day and can breed Legionella, so the version that works is a thin film down glass.
builds.line: As filmed it is a 12,000 gallon-an-hour indoor rainstorm; a slow film down glass, sanitized and on a GFCI, is a reasonable weekend-plus project.

builds.title: The mud pizza oven: can you build it Saturday and bake on Sunday?
builds.dek: Reels make a cob oven look like an afternoon of stomping mud and a same-night pizza; the oven is real, but the timeline is weeks, and it needs a base, insulation and a roof.
builds.line: The oven is real and cheap; the same-day firing is not, and rain will melt it without a roof.

builds.title: The hillside hobbit house: can you dig a home into a hill yourself?
builds.dek: A round green door in a grassy bank is the most charming build on the feed, but a roof of wet earth weighs as much as a fleet of trucks, and the real versions are built of concrete.
builds.line: The timber-and-turf hut in the clip is a slow collapse; a concrete shell built into the hill, sealed and drained, is a real and comfortable house.

builds.title: The old-window greenhouse: charming, cheap and a little dangerous?
builds.dek: A greenhouse pieced together from salvaged windows is one of the feed's prettiest builds; the walls can work, but the glass roof, the old paint and the missing vents need fixing first.
builds.line: As filmed it is a glass roof over your head and an oven by noon; with a plastic roof, vents and a real frame, the walls of old windows make a fine greenhouse.

builds.title: The chlorine-free swimming pond: do plants really keep it clean?
builds.dek: Reels show a backyard hole turned into a crystal-clear plant-filtered pond in a weekend; the idea is sound, but only with a plant zone as big as the swim zone, a sealed liner and a season or two of patience.
builds.line: As filmed it is a garden pond that will turn green; sized and built right, a plant-filtered pond is a proven way to swim without chlorine.

builds.title: The floor-to-ceiling aquarium wall: can a living room hold one?
builds.dek: A wall of water from floor to ceiling looks effortless in the reel, but it weighs eight tons and needs a window three inches thick, so the version that works is waist-high with a room behind it.
builds.line: Floor to ceiling, it overloads the floor and hides its own plumbing; waist-high in a framed wall with a service room behind, it is a proven build.

builds.title: The cinder block hot tub: can a fire under a stock tank make a spa?
builds.dek: A steel stock tank perched on a ring of cinder blocks with a fire roaring underneath makes a cozy reel; built that way it scorches, sags and overheats, but a tank with a side-mounted heater works.
builds.line: As filmed it is a cooking pot with people in it; on a full pad with a side heater and a thermometer, it is a fine soak.

builds.title: A shipping container buried in the backyard is a bunker waiting to cave in
builds.dek: Reels show a steel box dropped in a hole and covered over as a secret room, but a container's roof and walls were never meant to hold back soil, and the air inside runs out fast.
builds.line: A bare buried container is a crushing and suffocation hazard; the only safe version puts it inside an engineered concrete vault, and that is a contractor job.

builds.title: The soda-bottle garden tower: can a column of bottles feed you?
builds.dek: A stack of cut plastic bottles on a fence, bursting with lettuce and strawberries, is a feed favorite; as shown it would dry out by afternoon, but a post-mounted, drip-fed version is a proven extension design.
builds.line: As filmed the bottles hold about a day of water and cook in the sun; painted, post-mounted and drip-fed, the tower is a real, cheap garden.

builds.title: The bedroom with a window into the pool: could you dig one yourself?
builds.dek: Reels show a shovel, some concrete and a sheet of glass turning a backyard into an underwater lounge; done that way it is a room that can flood in seconds, and only an engineered, professional-led version is safe.
builds.line: As filmed it is a flood trap; engineered and professionally built it is real, but it is a six-figure project, not a weekend dig.

builds.title: The plastic bottle pool: could you build the viral reel?
builds.dek: A backyard pool walled with thousands of water bottles and a skin of cement racks up likes. Filled, it would let go all at once, but a round, footed version can work.
builds.line: As filmed it is a wall, not a pool; round, footed and lined, it becomes a real project.
